title: Seeing Triple
caption: Galaxy cluster RX J2129, imaged by the James Webb Space Telescope

recognition.text: ESA/Webb Picture of the Month (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: Mostly reddish stars and galaxies are scattered across a dark background. In the upper right, a large elliptical galaxy with a bright center and a diffuse white glow sits among many smaller, similar galaxies, and around it are distorted images and arcs of light. This is the massive galaxy cluster RX J2129, photographed by Webb.

The cluster is heavy enough to bend space around it, so it acts like a vast lens for light passing through from behind. The concentric arcs are background objects stretched by this gravitational lensing. The effect is so strong that the picture contains three separate images of one distant galaxy, which hosts a supernova.

Hubble spotted that supernova first, and astronomers suspected it was a very distant Type Ia. Such explosions shine with a fairly consistent brightness, so how dim one appears reveals its distance, making them useful 'standard candles'.
scale: The lensing cluster RX J2129 lies around 3.2 billion light-years from Earth, according to ESA/Webb.

understand.summary: This infrared image was taken with Webb's Near-InfraRed Camera (NIRCam). Light at 1.15 and 1.5 microns is shown in blue, 2.0 and 2.77 microns in green, and 3.56 and 4.44 microns in red.
understand.eye: All of this light is infrared, invisible to the human eye, so the colors are a translation of wavelengths we cannot see.

explore: Because the supernova's true brightness is roughly known, it can also show how strongly RX J2129 magnifies things behind it, and so how massive the cluster is. In effect, it measures the lens's 'prescription'.
Webb's NIRCam measured the supernova's brightness, and NIRSpec took its spectrum, so it can be compared with Type Ia supernovae in the nearby Universe to check a trusted distance method.
alt: Reddish galaxies on a dark background, with a large bright elliptical galaxy in the upper right surrounded by smaller galaxies and curved arcs of light.
